blurb: What happens between hitting send and seeing words appear — and the tricks that make it fast and cheap.

cards.title: What happens when you hit send

steps.h: Read the whole prompt at once
steps.p: First the model processes your entire prompt in one go. This "prefill" phase is quick per word, because the GPU can work on all the words in parallel.
steps.analogy: Taking in a whole page at a glance.

steps.h: Then write one token at a time
steps.p: Next comes "decode": the model produces the answer one token at a time, and each new token needs another full pass through the model.

visual.caption: Each token has to wait for the one before it.

steps.p: For every new token, the GPU must read all of the model's billions of numbers from memory. Moving that data, not doing the maths, is usually what takes the time.
steps.analogy: A chef who must walk to a far-off store room for every ingredient, for every single dish.

steps.p: So it doesn't redo work on earlier words, the model saves notes about every token so far. This KV cache grows with every word in the conversation.
Servers batch many users' requests together: one trip to memory for the model's numbers produces the next token for dozens of people.

visual.caption: One read of the model, many users served.

cards.q: You paste a very long document and ask a question. What mostly decides how long you wait before the first word appears?
options: Prefill: reading the whole prompt (plus any queue)
How long the answer will be
The size of the text on your screen
How many people liked the answer
cards.hint: What has to happen before any answer can start?
cards.why: Prefill. The model must read your whole prompt before writing anything. A huge document means a longer read; after that, words appear at the decode speed.

cards.statement: AI companies usually charge more per output token than per input token.
cards.why: True. Input is read in one fast, parallel pass. Output is written one token at a time, each needing a full trip through the model. Output often costs several times more.

cards.q: Why do servers handle many users' requests together?
options: One read of the model's numbers can produce the next token for many users
So everyone waits exactly the same time
Because GPUs only work when completely full
To share users' chats with each other
cards.hint: Remember the chef and the store room.
cards.why: Share the expensive trip. Fetching the model's numbers is the slow part. Doing it once for dozens of requests makes each answer far cheaper. Your chats stay separate.

cards.q: What does the KV cache store?
options: The model's notes about earlier tokens, so they aren't recomputed
A copy of the internet
Your saved chats for next week
The model's training data
cards.why: Notes on earlier tokens. Without them, every new word would mean re-reading the whole conversation from scratch. The catch: the notes take memory, growing with every word.

cards.title: A popular serving tool, vLLM, borrowed a trick from computer operating systems to manage the KV cache.
cards.detail: It stores each conversation's notes in small fixed-size blocks — like the memory "pages" your computer uses — instead of one big reserved chunk. Less wasted memory means more users per GPU.

cards.statement: Prompt caching lets a provider skip re-reading the start of a prompt it has seen recently.
cards.why: True. If many requests begin with the same long instructions or document, the provider keeps their KV cache and reuses it. It's faster, and cached input is usually billed at a discount.

steps.h: A model is a pile of numbers
steps.p: Every parameter is a number, usually stored in 16 bits (2 bytes). So a 70-billion-parameter model needs about 140 GB just to hold its numbers — more than any single normal GPU.
Quantization stores each number with fewer bits — 8, or even 4 — by rounding it to the nearest of a smaller set of allowed values.
steps.analogy: Rounding prices to the nearest 10p: you lose a little detail, but the total barely changes.

steps.p: 8 bits halves the memory; 4 bits cuts it to a quarter. A model that needed several data-centre GPUs can then fit on one card.
Writing each token means reading every number from memory. Smaller numbers mean less to read, so answers come out faster.
Round too hard and quality drops. Modern methods are clever about it — for example, keeping a few important numbers more precise — so 4-bit models usually lose surprisingly little.

cards.q: A 70-billion-parameter model stored at 4 bits per number needs roughly how much memory for its weights?
options: 35 GB
140 GB
70 GB
4 GB
cards.hint: 4 bits = half a byte. 70 billion × ½ byte = ?
cards.why: About 35 GB. 70 billion numbers × half a byte each = 35 billion bytes. Real files are slightly bigger, because some extra scaling numbers are stored too.

cards.statement: Shrinking a big model to 4 bits usually ruins its quality.
cards.why: False. With good methods, 4-bit versions of large models typically lose only a little accuracy. Smaller models and very hard tasks suffer more, so it's worth testing.

cards.q: Why does quantization make answers come out faster?
options: There are fewer bytes to read from memory for every token
The model skips half its layers
It deletes words from your prompt
It speeds up the GPU's clock
cards.hint: What's the slow part of writing each token?
cards.why: Less to fetch. Each new token needs every weight read from memory. Halving the bytes roughly halves that reading time when one person is using the model.

cards.title: Ollama, which runs AI models on your own laptop, was built on llama.cpp — a project that began as a weekend hack.
cards.detail: In March 2023 developer Georgi Gerganov wrote llama.cpp to run Meta's LLaMA model on a MacBook using 4-bit numbers. It became one of the most popular ways to run models locally.

cards.q: Early attempts to round big models to 8 bits hit a snag. What was it?
options: A few internal values were huge, and rounding wrecked the rest
GPUs couldn't count past 8
The models refused to run
Answers came out in another language
cards.hint: One giant number makes it hard to round all the small ones.
cards.why: Outliers. In large models a handful of internal signals get enormous values. Rounding everything to fit them flattens the small values. The 2022 LLM.int8() method fixed this by keeping those outliers more precise.

cards.statement: Quantization can let a model run on hardware that couldn't hold the original.
cards.why: True. That's its biggest use: a 4-bit model needs about a quarter of the memory, which is how decent models run on laptops and phones.

steps.p: While writing one token at a time, the GPU spends most of its time fetching the model's numbers from memory. Its maths units sit mostly idle.
A small, quick "draft" model races ahead and guesses the next few tokens — say, five.
steps.analogy: An intern drafts the next sentence; the senior writer only has to check it.

steps.p: The big model checks all five guesses in a single pass. That costs about the same as writing one token, because its numbers are fetched from memory only once.

visual.caption: Three guesses accepted, one corrected — four tokens for the price of one.

steps.p: Guesses are accepted up to the first one the big model disagrees with. It supplies the right token there, and drafting starts again from that point.
The acceptance rules make the final text match what the big model would have written alone — often 2–3× faster when the guesser is good.

cards.q: Why is checking five guessed tokens about as cheap as writing one?
options: The model's numbers are read from memory once and used for all five
The big model skips checking most of them
Short words cost nothing
The draft model does the checking
cards.hint: Remember which part of decoding is slow.
cards.why: One trip to memory. Decoding is limited by fetching the weights, not by maths. Once fetched, scoring five positions instead of one barely adds time.

cards.statement: Speculative decoding changes the answer the big model would have given.
cards.why: False. The big model has the final say on every token, and the acceptance rule is designed so the output matches what it would produce alone. It's purely a speed trick.

cards.q: If the big model rejects the draft's 2nd guess, what happens?
options: It keeps the 1st guess, writes its own 2nd token, and drafting restarts
It throws away the whole answer
It accepts every guess anyway
It asks you to choose
cards.hint: Look at the ✓ and ✗ boxes in step 3.
cards.why: Keep, correct, carry on. Everything before the first disagreement is kept, the big model supplies the right token, and the guesser starts drafting again from there.

cards.q: What mostly decides how much speculative decoding speeds things up?
options: How often the big model accepts the draft's guesses
How many people are using the app
How long ago the model was trained
Whether the answer contains numbers
cards.why: The acceptance rate. If most guesses are accepted, each check yields several tokens. If they're mostly rejected, you've paid for drafting and gained little. Predictable text — like code — speeds up most.

cards.title: Some models are trained to predict several future tokens at once.
cards.detail: DeepSeek-V3, for example, was trained to also predict the token after next. Those extra predictions can act as built-in drafts for speculative decoding.

cards.statement: Always picking the single most likely next token guarantees the most likely full answer.
cards.why: False. A slightly less likely word now can lead to a much more likely sentence overall. Picking the top word at each step (greedy decoding) is a shortcut, not a guarantee.

cards.title: How the model picks each word

steps.p: At each step the model gives every token it knows a probability. Something then has to pick one.
Picking the most likely word every time (greedy decoding) is predictable, but long writing can get dull and repetitive.
Instead, apps usually sample: pick at random, but in proportion to the probabilities. "sunny" wins half the time, "warm" about a third.
steps.analogy: A raffle where "sunny" holds 50 tickets, "warm" 30 and "purple" half of one.

steps.p: Temperature reshapes the odds before the draw. Low makes the favourite even stronger (safe and focused). High evens things out (more surprising, more risky).

visual.caption: Illustration: same menu, different dial setting.

steps.p: Top-p sampling only allows the most likely tokens that together make up, say, 90% of the probability. Rare oddities like "purple" can never be drawn.

cards.q: With top-p = 0.9, which tokens can be picked?
options: The smallest group of top tokens whose chances add up to 90%
Any token with at least a 9% chance
Exactly the top 9 tokens
Only the single most likely token
cards.hint: Add the chances up from the top until you reach 90%.
cards.why: The top 90% of the probability. Sort tokens from most to least likely and add their chances until you pass 0.9. Only those can be drawn, so the long tail of oddities is cut off.

cards.q: You want an AI to brainstorm wild, varied ideas. Which temperature?
options: Higher
Lower
Exactly zero
Temperature doesn't affect this
cards.why: Higher. It spreads the odds out, so less obvious words get picked more often. Great for ideas; worse for facts, where you want the safest answer.

cards.q: Why don't chatbots always pick the single most likely word?
options: It tends to make longer text dull and repetitive
It's too slow to work out
It's against the rules
The most likely word is usually wrong
cards.why: Dull, loopy text. Always taking the safest word can make writing flat and send it into repeated phrases. A little randomness keeps it natural.

cards.statement: Setting temperature to 0 guarantees exactly the same answer every time from an AI service.
cards.hint: Servers batch and round numbers in slightly different ways.
cards.why: False. It makes choices near-greedy, but tiny differences in how servers batch and round numbers can still flip a token — and once one word changes, the rest can follow.

cards.title: Apps can force a model to reply in a strict format, like valid JSON.
cards.detail: At each step, the software blocks any token that would break the format, so only valid choices remain. It's called constrained decoding — handy when another program has to read the reply.

cards.title: Match temperature to the task
cards.body: Use low temperature for facts, maths and code, where there's one right answer. Use higher for brainstorming, names and creative writing, where variety helps.
cards.challenge: Ask an AI for 10 names for a café. Then ask again, adding "be wildly creative", and compare the variety.
